subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: I'm Lalremsiami, and I sit next to Damini in Class 5. On Career Day, Miss asked us to draw what we'd be. Damini drew a doctor with a stethoscope before Miss had even finished speaking. "My grandfather was a doctor, my mother is a doctor, so I'm going to be a doctor," she told the whole row, chin up. When Miss asked, "What do you like about it?" Damini said, "Everyone in my family is one," and looked surprised that there could be another kind of answer. At lunch she drew rockets on her tiffin napkin, like she always does. I don't know what's in her head. But she said the word doctor the way you say your own name.

qa.q: What did Damini draw on her tiffin napkin at lunch?
qa.a: Rockets.

qa.q: Why did Damini look surprised when Miss asked what she liked about being a doctor?
qa.a: She had never questioned the plan; it came from her family, so she hadn't thought there could be another kind of answer.

qa.q: What could Miss try next, given the rockets on the napkin?
qa.a: Miss could ask Damini about the rockets too, opening space to explore her own interests while still respecting the doctor plan.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see the way Damini says 'doctor'?
qa.a: Lalremsiami notices Damini says it like her own name, as something given and certain, while admitting not knowing what Damini really thinks.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl proudly announce she will be a doctor because her family are doctors, a role handed to her that no one has questioned.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: Saturday. At the family dinner, Imran, eight, stood on his chair. "I'm going to be an engineer, like Abbu and Parveen Khala!" Everyone clapped. Abbu ruffled his hair, and Imran glowed all night. Tuesday. His teacher asked the class why they wanted their jobs. Imran said, "Because I'm going to be an engineer." "But why?" asked a classmate. Imran frowned. "Because... I just am." Friday. Parveen Khala was fixing her laptop at the dining table. "Do you like building things, Imran?" He thought. "I like drawing birds." She smiled. "Birds are good too." Imran looked at her, then at his drawing book, puzzled and somehow lighter.

qa.q: What did Imran say he likes when Parveen Khala asked about building things?
qa.a: He likes drawing birds.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when the classmate asked 'But why?'
qa.a: He was confused; he had never thought about it, because the plan came from his family and no one had questioned it.

qa.q: What choice did Parveen Khala make on Friday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She asked what Imran actually likes and welcomed his answer about birds, giving him room to explore beyond the role handed to him.

qa.q: What would change if the family had clapped just as loudly for birds?
qa.a: Imran might feel free to explore his own interests, since his pride would no longer rest only on the engineer plan.

grounding: A boy proudly repeats the engineer plan his family expects, cannot explain it when questioned, and feels lighter when his aunt asks what he likes.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: Vaibhav Dadu smiled at his granddaughter. "You want to know why I became a teacher and not a doctor, Yamini? When I was nine, in our house in Nagpur, everybody asked me, 'What will you become?' I would stand straight and say, 'Doctor!' My father smiled, my aunts pinched my cheek. It felt wonderful. Nobody argued, so I never wondered. It was like wearing my elder cousin's school blazer: it came to me already made. Then at twelve, a neighbour asked me to explain the stars to her little ones on the terrace, and I talked for an hour. That night I understood that 'doctor' was a word I carried, not a thing I had chosen. It took me years to say so aloud."

qa.q: What did Vaibhav explain to the neighbour's little ones on the terrace?
qa.a: The stars.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel as a nine-year-old saying 'Doctor!'?
qa.a: It felt wonderful; he enjoyed the smiles and cheek-pinching, and since nobody argued he never wondered about it.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Vaibhav, and what did he understand?
qa.a: Talking about the stars for an hour at twelve; he understood that 'doctor' was a word he carried, not something he had chosen.

qa.q: Why might Dadu tell Yamini this story now?
qa.a: Yamini asked why he became a teacher, and he may want her to know she can explore her own path rather than carry one handed to her.

grounding: A grandfather recalls proudly repeating the doctor plan his family gave him as a boy, a borrowed role that felt safe until a new interest showed it was not his own.

passage:
The lights went out at seven, and Jatin's essay, "My Aim in Life", was due tomorrow. By the candle on the dining table he wrote in his best letters: I will be an engineer like Papa and Ramesh Chacha.
"Good boy," said Ramesh Chacha, holding the candle closer. Jatin wrote the same sentence again at the end and underlined it twice. Wax dripped onto the page, and he scraped it off carefully.
From the sofa, his little cousin Pinky asked, "What does an engineer do all day?"
Jatin thought. "Big things. Bridges. Papa knows." He bent over his page again, proud and calm. Nobody at home had ever asked him what else he might like, and in the dark it felt good to be so sure.

qa.q: What was the title of Jatin's essay?
qa.a: The title was My Aim in Life.

qa.q: Why did being so sure feel good to Jatin in the dark?
qa.a: The plan came ready-made from Papa and Ramesh Chacha, nobody questioned it, and the praise made him feel safe and proud.

qa.q: At the moment Jatin answered Pinky, what could an adult have asked to help him start exploring?
qa.a: They could ask what he likes about bridges, or what else he enjoys, so the goal becomes something he looks into rather than just repeats.

qa.q: How might Pinky's question look to Ramesh Chacha if he really listened?
qa.a: He might notice that Jatin knows little about the job he claims, and wonder whether the aim is truly Jatin's own.

grounding: A boy writes with pride that he will be an engineer like his father and uncle, a goal handed to him that nobody questions.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
At the Children's Day programme in the party hall of their Kochi apartment block, Elizabeth Aunty held the microphone out to each child. "And what will you become?"
Salma, eleven, didn't even pause. "A chartered accountant, like my Umma and Uppa. I'll join their office." Several aunties clapped, and her Uppa, in the second row, raised his tea cup.
"What do you like best about accounts, Salma?"
Salma blinked. "It's... a very good job. Everybody in our family says so." She said it louder, and the clapping came again.
Back in her seat she swung her legs, pleased. The question about liking it had slid off her like rain off the balcony glass. Nobody asked it twice.

qa.q: What did Salma say she would become?
qa.a: A chartered accountant, like her Umma and Uppa.

qa.q: How does Salma feel about her answer, and what does her blink suggest?
qa.a: She feels pleased and sure of her answer, yet her blink suggests she had never thought about what she actually likes in the job.

qa.q: What could Salma's parents do later that evening to help her explore without taking away her pride?
qa.a: They could ask what she enjoys at school and mention other paths too, so accounts becomes a choice she tests, not only one she repeats.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth Aunty have noticed that the clapping crowd didn't?
qa.a: That Salma could name the job but not one reason she likes it, a sign the goal is borrowed rather than explored.

grounding: An eleven-year-old proudly announces the family career as her own, and the question of whether she likes it slides past unexamined.
